title: KV fragmentation budgeting and bump-refill playbook
body:
Summary:

This doc proposes an operational "fragmentation budget" layer and a light-weight bump-pointer refill strategy for the KV cache to reduce long-tail memory waste and make compaction/reclaim behavior more predictable across mixed workloads. The approach bundles three pieces: 1) per-shard fragmentation accounting and budget enforcement; 2) a "bump-refill" fast-path for satisfying small allocations from reserved contiguous bump ranges to avoid scattering; and 3) a conservative background merge/compaction loop that targets shards exceeding their fragmentation budgets.

Motivation / observed problems:

- We observe sporadic memory pressure from highly-churny prefixes where many small entries are repeatedly inserted/evicted, causing fragmentation in slabless pools and ballooning RSS over time.
- Existing global compaction triggers are noisy: either they run too frequently (costly CPU/IO) or too rarely (OOM risk).
- Aggressive per-request allocation strategies reduce allocation latency but cause fragmentation when many small free holes appear interleaved with live KV pages.
- Current eviction (LRU-ish / hotness) doesn't reason about physical layout: evicting logical entries doesn't necessarily free contiguous physical spans for reuse.

Design goals:

- Limit fragmentation growth predictably per shard/tenant and convert fragmentation from an unbounded tail into a controllable signal (the "fragmentation budget").
- Maintain low allocation path latency for common-case small allocations.
- Avoid forcing global stop-the-world compaction; prefer targeted background work focusing on shards that violate budgets.
- Provide telemetry and knobs to tune per-tenant budgets, and provide graceful fallback when budgets are exhausted.

Core concepts:

1) Fragmentation accounting (per-shard):
   - Maintain two counters per shard: allocated_logical_bytes and allocated_physical_bytes. Fragmentation = physical - logical.
   - Track a rolling 1h/6h/24h moving-average of fragmentation to avoid reacting to spikes.
   - Each shard has a configurable fragmentation_budget (absolute bytes and ratio to logical bytes).

2) Fragmentation budget enforcement:
   - Normal allocations proceed as today (fast-path). When a shard's fragmentation exceeds budget, the shard enters "constrained" mode and new large allocations (> threshold) are subject to fallback paths (e.g., steal from a global reserve or trigger an async reclaim).
   - Small allocations can continue using bump-refill if available to avoid latency regressions.

3) Bump-pointer refill (fast-path contiguous reserve):
   - Each shard maintains a small set of bump ranges (contiguous virtual spans) pre-allocated from the slabless pool. Allocations that fit within the current bump range are O(1) pointer bump.
   - When a bump range is exhausted, instead of immediately requesting many small new spans (which increases scattering), the allocator either: (a) top-up from a small per-shard refill reserve (single contiguous chunk), or (b) if refill not available, allocate from the general pool and mark the fragment metadata to prefer nearby merges.
   - Bump ranges are intentionally sized to balance worst-case fragmentation vs allocation latency — e.g., typical size 64KB - 256KB for small-value workloads.

4) Proactive merge / background compaction loop:
   - Background worker(s) periodically scan shards with fragmentation > budget. For each target shard, attempt cheap coalesces: reclaim dead ranges, defragment adjacent small holes into contiguous ranges, and merge into a small number of free spans suitable for future bump refills.
   - Work is rate-limited by a shard-specific compaction_credit meter that replenishes slowly and is charged on compaction CPU/time. The credit ties into tenant/capacity accounting so noisy tenants pay for their defrag work.

5) Reclamation vs eviction coordination:
   - Eviction heuristics are augmented to prefer removing entries that lead to physically contiguous freed spans when fragmentation is high — i.e., an eviction score gets a small bonus for entries lying adjacent to existing free holes to enable larger contiguous free spans. This is a soft bias to avoid thrashing.

6) Global reserve and emergency fallbacks:
   - A small global contiguous reserve (per-machine) for large allocations can be used when shards are constrained; usage is metered and charged back to the shard so long-term reliance forces operator intervention.

Instrumentation / metrics to surface:

- shard_fragmentation_bytes / shard_logical_bytes (gauge)
- shard_fragmentation_ratio (gauge)
- fragment_budget_threshold (config) and times_exceeded (counter)
- bump_range_hit_rate (ratio of small allocs satisfied via bump)
- compaction_cycles_per_shard (counter) and compaction_cpu_ms (histogram)
- reclaimed_bytes_per_cycle
- eviction_physical_coalescence_score (histogram of how often eviction freed contiguous runs)
- tenant_compaction_cost_charge (counter)

Heuristics and knobs (initial defaults):

- fragmentation_budget: min(16MB, 10% of logical bytes), floor 1MB.
- bump_range_size: 128KB default for small-value workloads; allow tuning per-shard based on median value size.
- refill_reserve_size: 256KB per shard soft reserve.
- large_allocation_threshold: >= 4KB (alloc larger than this triggers different path).
- compaction_credit_replenish: 1 credit / minute; each compaction cycle costs ~1 credit (tunable).

Algorithmic notes / pseudocode (allocation path):

- allocate(size, shard):
    if size <= small_threshold and bump_range.has_space(size):
      ptr = bump_range.alloc(size); bump_range_hit++ ; return ptr
    if shard.fragmentation < budget:
      ptr = general_allocator.alloc(size); update physical/accounting; return ptr
    else:
      if size <= small_threshold and shard.refill_reserve.has_space(size):
         ptr = shard.refill_reserve.alloc(size); mark reservation; return ptr
      else if global_reserve.can_satisfy(size):
         charge(shard, size); return global_reserve.alloc(size)
      else:
         trigger_async_compaction(shard); return allocation_failure_or_slow_blocking_path

Background compaction (simplified):

- while compaction_worker.available():
    pick shard with fragmentation > budget and compaction_credit > 0
    scan free spans and adjacent live entries to identify coalescable regions
    try to relocate small live entries into nearby free space using cheap copies (bounded time)
    merge freed ranges into larger contiguous spans and return to slabless pool
    charge compaction cost to shard; decrement compaction_credit

Experiment plan / validation:

- Benchmarks: synthetic workloads that stress small entry churn, mixed-size workloads, and sequential-scanner workloads. Compare RSS, alloc latency, and compaction CPU between baseline and new approach.
- Canary rollout: enable fragmentation budgeting in read-only mode for a small subset of shards (observe metric trends) -> enable enforcement with bump-refill for 5% traffic -> 25% -> full.
- Failure scenarios: ensure global_reserve exhaustion is instrumented and triggers safe fallback (reject large allocations with clear error; route to lower-tier storage).

Operational concerns:

- Accounting: compaction work must be chargeable to tenants so a noisy tenant can't indefinitely push cost onto others. Tie compaction_charge to billing reports.
- QoS: in constrained mode, prioritize read/critical traffic and push best-effort compaction as background.
- Debugging: add per-shard fragmentation timelines and a flamegraph-like view mapping allocation hot ranges to physical spans to help triage.

Open questions / TODOs:

- What is the right default bump_range size across different model workloads? Need microbenchmarks profiling typical value sizes (embed cache vs tokenized prompts).
- How aggressive should eviction coalescence bias be before it harms cache hit quality? We need A/B tests.
- Should we enable relocation of live entries (copying) aggressively or rely primarily on eviction+compaction of dead ranges? Relocation reduces fragmentation faster but can be expensive CPU.
- Integrations: tie compaction charges to existing billing pipeline and Redwood Console dashboards.

Next steps / short-term action items:

- (Ravi) implement lightweight per-shard fragmentation counters + bump_range prototype (2 weeks)
- (Dana) create benchmark harness for churny small-entry workloads and run baseline vs bump-refill (1 week)
- (Marco) wire metrics to telemetry and build a simple dashboard to spot shards exceeding budget (1 week)
- Follow-up: implement background compaction worker and compaction_credit metering (RFC after prototype results).

Notes to reviewers:

This is intentionally conservative — the goal is to convert an unbounded operational tail (fragmentation growth) into a controllable, observable signal with predictable mitigation steps. The bump-refill mechanism keeps small-allocation latency low while making defragmentation more feasible and focused. Feedback welcome on heuristics and whether to try more aggressive relocation early in the prototype.

References / links:

- Experiment notes: slack thread #kv-cache-arch 2024-11-10
- Benchmark harness: github: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/tree/main/bench/churn-tests
- Related RFCs: KV-allocator-design (Confluence)
